title: Microservice architecture
idea: Microservices split an application into small services, each with one job and its own data. Services deploy on their own and talk over the network.

analogy.text: A food court. Each stall cooks one kind of food, runs its own kitchen and can open or close alone. Ordering a full meal means visiting several stalls.
analogy.breaks: Services call each other while handling one request, and those calls can fail.

points: Each service owns one capability and its own data, reached only through its API.
Teams deploy and scale each service independently.
Calls between services are network requests, so they can be slow or fail.
A change that spans services cannot use a single database transaction.

steps.caption: Clients send every request to one entry point, a gateway that routes by path.
The gateway routes the request to the Orders service.
Orders needs a payment, so it calls Payments over the network.
Each service writes only to its own database. Orders never reads the Payments database.
Payments goes down. The Users service keeps running, and Orders does too if it handles the failed call.
Payments is back, and traffic grows on Orders alone.
Only Orders runs more copies. Users and Payments stay as they are.

code.title: Same call, over the network
code.caption: In the monolith this was a function call. Now it is a network request that can fail.

walk.text: Payments is its own small HTTP server. It always answers `paid`.
Listen on a free port and build its URL.
Orders makes a network request and handles a failed call in `catch`.
Payments is running, so the call succeeds.
Stop Payments, as a crash or a deploy would.
The same call now fails, and Orders still returns an answer.

pitfalls: Do not share one database between services; that couples them again.
Do not split early; more services mean more to deploy, monitor and debug.
Never assume a call to another service succeeds; plan for it to fail.

quiz.q: What does the script print, line by line?
options: order paid, then order failed: payments unreachable
quiz.why: The first call reaches the running service. After `close()` the port refuses connections, `fetch` rejects, and `catch` returns the failure message.

takeaway: Microservices buy independence at the price of network calls and more to operate.

starters: How small should a microservice be?
How do services find each other?
How do I handle a transaction that spans two services?
